Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

name: AHT Founders Exhibition Year 2: The ArtBarn
description:
The Visual Arts Building (aka the Art Barn), which closed in 2013 and was torn down in 2017, served as an incubator for the visual arts, involving the campus community, the larger DFW community, and beyond. Students entered the classroom by walking through the gallery, which represented one of the strongest characteristics of the building. This openness served as an invitation to artists who exhibited in the gallery, with the potential to explore these large spaces coupled with high ceilings, complemented by a viewing area located on the second floor. Over the years, classes and facilities supported a variety of mediums: painting, drawing, photography, printmaking, sculpture, and design; and at different times, ceramics, video, computer imaging, laser cutting, and robotics. Arts faculty curated most of the exhibitions and experienced a unique level of autonomy, while students had unparalleled access to exhibition spaces and facilities. Altogether, the building’s design helped to facilitate a strong sense of community that has continued to reverberate over many decades.

Join us October 6–10, 2025 in the ATC 3rd Floor Gallery, open daily from 9 AM to 5 PM, as we celebrate the rich history of the ArtBarn Visual Arts Building. Explore a vibrant showcase of faculty and student work, event footage, and reflections on the origins of what has become the modern-day Visual Arts Program at UT Dallas.

name: Chemistry Seminar - Life of a Molecule: from Chemical Reactivity to Bedside
description: Our research program spans the spectrum from uncovering fundamental principles of chemical reactivity to applying these insights in biomedical contexts. The ability to design and construct new molecular architectures with defined properties critically depends on efficient methods for controlled and selective bond formation in complex environments. Transformations that reliably introduce or interconvert functional groups are essential for synthesizing materials ranging from small-molecule therapeutics to multifunctional macromolecular systems for imaging and targeted drug delivery. Catalysis offers unparalleled opportunities to achieve these goals while sharpening and training the chemist’s intuition, the quiet engine behind the capacity to recognize patterns of reactivity, anticipate new transformations, and design molecules that push the boundaries of function. This presentation will highlight our work on discovering and understanding new catalytic reactions, elucidating underlying mechanisms and catalyst behavior, and translating these findings into practical applications in drug discovery, cellular and tissue imaging, and precision therapeutics.

name: Data Science and Statistics Seminar by Dr. Changwoo Lee
description: Title: Scalable and robust regression models for continuous proportional data Abstract: Beta regression is used routinely for continuous proportional data, but it often encounters practical issues such as a lack of robustness of regression parameter estimates to misspecification of the beta distribution. We develop an improved class of generalized linear models starting with the continuous binomial (cobin) distribution and further extending to dispersion mixtures of cobin distributions (micobin). The proposed cobin regression and micobin regression models have attractive robustness, computation, and flexibility properties. A key innovation is the Kolmogorov-Gamma data augmentation scheme, which facilitates Gibbs sampling for Bayesian computation, including in hierarchical cases involving nested, longitudinal, or spatial data. We demonstrate robustness, ability to handle responses exactly at the boundary (0 or 1), and computational efficiency relative to beta regression in simulation experiments and through analysis of the benthic macroinvertebrate multimetric index of US lakes using lake watershed covariates.

name: Learning to Communicate
description:
Dr. Robert Calderbank

Charles S Sydnor Distinguished Professor

 

It is common knowledge that a time-domain pulse is well adapted to pure delay channels, and that a frequency domain pulse is well adapted to pure Doppler channels. In this talk we will explain why the Zak-OTFS waveform, a pulse in the delay-Doppler domain, is well adapted to the doubly spread channels that arise in wireless communication. We will describe how to design the Zak-OTFS waveform so that the input-output (IO) relation is predictable and non-fading, and we will explain how it is possible to learn the IO relation without needing to estimate the underlying channel. We will explore the possibility of a model-free mode of operation, which is especially useful when a traditional model-dependent mode of operation (reliant on channel estimation) is out of reach. We will also describe how the Zak-OTFS waveform supports combined communication and sensing by enabling unambiguous delay-Doppler estimation.

This is joint work with Saif Mohammed, Ananthanarayanan Chockalingam, and Ronny Hadani.

name: Early Vocabulary Development in Children With IDD and Autistic Children Who Use AAC — Callier FLASH Seminar
description:
Callier FLASH Seminar in Speech, Language and Hearing

Title: Early Vocabulary Development in Children With IDD and Autistic Children Who Use AAC

Speaker: Courtney Trevino, PhD, CCC-SLP
Texas Christian University

Dr. Trevino’s line of work examines early vocabulary development in children who use augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), with focus on word learning and lexical integration. This presentation will review outcomes from studies involving children with intellectual and/or developmental disabilities and autistic children who use AAC. Theoretical and clinical implications will be discussed, along with future directions informed by these outcomes.

Courtney Trevino, PhD, CCC-SLP is a Postdoctoral Fellow in the CHLLD Lab (PI: Dr. Emily Lund) in the Davies School of Communication Sciences and Disorders at Texas Christian University. Dr. Trevino completed her Bachelor of Science in Communication Sciences and Disorders (2015), Master of Science in Speech Language Pathology (2017), and PhD in Health Sciences (with emphasis in speech-language pathology; 2024). She also practiced in a rural school district (as the AAC Team Lead) for four years prior to returning to academia to pursue her PhD. Dr. Trevino’s line of work focuses on early word learning and lexical integration in children with IDD and autistic children who use AAC. Her Postdoctoral Fellow experience has expanded her work to include children who are deaf or hard of hearing, semantic development past early stages, and longitudinal methodology.

name: Using “Sidewalk Neuroscience” to Study Power Relationships — Frontiers of BrainHealth Lecture
description:

Using “Sidewalk Neuroscience” to Study Power Relationships

Patrick A. Stewart, PhD
University of Arkansas

“Sidewalk neuroscience” refers to gaining insights into the function of human behavior through simple observation; as a result, this form of scientific discovery is available to all and, if rigorously applied, can provide insights into human emotions and behavioral intent. In this presentation, political scientist Dr. Patrick A. Stewart discusses how observing and coding the behavior of public figures by using the Ethological Coding System for Interviews (ECSI) and eye blink rates can provide insights into power relationships.

Dr. Patrick A. Stewart currently teaches graduate and undergraduate classes at the University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, where he is a professor and director of online education in the Department of Political Science. Read more.

name: Reflecting Nature Through Ink and Imagination: Artist Talk with Lam Tung Pang
description:
Join us for an artist talk with Lam Tung Pang, whose immersive installation Mountains de-bonding reimagines the legacy of Chinese landscape painting through contemporary materials and ecological reflection. Working in charcoal and ink on plywood, Lam blends historical reverence with modern experimentation, building monumental panels that echo the visual language of sacred mountain woodblock prints.

Lam will discuss how his training in Fine Arts, particularly at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, informs his creative practice today. From the use of humble materials like plywood to his interpretation of the shan shui tradition, Lam’s work reflects both the permanence and enduring beauty of mountains and the impermanence and fragility of the environments they symbolize. Drawing parallels between ancient techniques and present-day environmental concerns and materials, this talk invites viewers to consider the natural world as both inspiration and mirror.

Hong Kong born Lam Tung Pang, working as an artist between Hong Kong, London and Beijing in his early stage, now lives and works in North America and Hong Kong. Lam's coming-of-age coincides with drastic social changes, a result of his homeland’s decolonization from constitutional monarchy and new allegiance to China in a short span of time. Traversing between the media of painting, site-specific installation, sound and video, Lam’s playful practice arises from a curious imagination that recombines traditional iconography and vernacular elements, innovating with a myriad of found objects and images to form new practices that are often experimental in nature. Lam’s works engage the themes of collective memories and fleeting nostalgia, which articulate an ongoing negotiation of the overlapping city-state’s reality. In his allegorical landscapes, journeys and sceneries become essential passages connecting time and distance, longing and loss.

Lam’s work is collected by LACMA (Los Angeles), Asian Art Museum (San Francisco), Burger Collection, the Deutsche Bank, Royal Bank of Canada, Hong Kong Museum of Art (Hong Kong), Kadist Art Foundation (France and USA),  White Rabbit Contemporary Chinese Art Collection (Australia) and M+ (Hong Kong), among others.

Doors will open at 10:30 a.m. 

Parking is free in lot M East

Have questions for the artist? Email them to crowexperience@crowmuseum.org for the chance to have it answered during the Q&A portion of this program.

Free with registration.

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

Athenaeum hours: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday. Free admission.

name: Leveraging Neuronal Activity-Dependent Processes to Produce Durable Plasticity After Injury - Neuroscience Seminar Series
description:
Neuroscience Seminar Series

Title: Leveraging Neuronal Activity-Dependent Processes to Produce Durable Plasticity After Injury

Speaker:
John H. Martin, PhD
City University of New York School of Medicine

The sudden loss of movement after a stroke or spinal cord injury (SCI) is life-changing. In a moment, the injured person can lose independence, becoming reliant on care-givers for daily activities.  Paralysis after stroke and SCI is a major impetus to study motor system plasticity, to develop novel repair strategies that rewire the damaged motor system and promote functional recovery. The motor cortex and the corticospinal tract are key to producing voluntary movements. In health and after injury, the spinal cord is an important site for activity-dependent plasticity of the corticospinal tract. My laboratory uses animal models to study activity-dependent axon outgrowth and synaptic plasticity that can be augmented by motor cortex and spinal cord neuromodulation to promote motor function after injury. My presentation will focus on the corticospinal motor system. I will talk about our research on how motor cortex neuromodulation can be used to upregulate molecular programs for axon growth and synaptogenesis and, in turn, promote activity-dependent corticospinal axon sprouting, synaptogenesis, and long-term potentiation (LTP) at the corticospinal tract-spinal neuron synapse in the spinal cord. I will focus on several rodent injury models, and show how neuromodulation approaches can be used to repair the damaged corticospinal system, reestablish key physiological processes, and promote recovery of skilled movements after SCI.

name: 13th Annual Anlin Ku Lecture
description:
The 13th Annual Anlin Ku Lecture features Dr. Denis Simon, a distinguished fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, on “Evolving U.S.-China Relations in an Era of Geo-Political Tensions: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives.”

Over the last decade, the U.S.-China relationship has moved in a decidedly contentious direction. The tensions largely have been driven by pronounced changes in the geopolitical environment as well as changes in the trade and investment relations between the two countries. At the core of these changes has been the rapid acceleration of China’s economic and technological advance.  Simply stated, China is no longer “the factory to the world” or an innovation laggard. Rather, it is well on its way to becoming an innovation powerhouse. As a result, China is increasingly viewed as an actual or potential strategic competitor of the U.S. Some U.S. officials have even gone as far as suggesting that China’s rapid rise represents an existential threat to the well-being and future prosperity of the United States.

The significant changes in the nature and tone of the bilateral relationship have raised both short-term and long-term concerns about the future trajectory of Sino-US relations. How will US-China relations evolve in the future? How will current tensions affect future cooperation in the fields of higher education and student exchanges, research collaboration in science and technology, and national security affairs? Is the prospect of military conflict as real as some analysts have suggested?

Professor Denis Simon will address these issues by providing insights from his four-plus decades of deep involvement in U.S.-China relations. Having first visited China in 1981 and having lived in Beijing and Shanghai on three separate occasions, Professor Simon has seen China from the perspective of a research scholar, a high-level corporate executive, and a senior academic administrator. Through the lens of his extensive experience and knowledge, he will provide guidance about what to expect from what some observers have suggested is “the most important bilateral relationship” in the world.

6:30 PM - Reception
7:30 PM - Lecture

RSVP Here

Denis Simon is an expert on international science and technology affairs.  He has more than four decades of experience studying business, competition, innovation, and talent strategy in China. From 2015-2022, he served as professor of practice at Duke University’s Fuqua School of Business and executive vice chancellor of Duke Kunshan University in China from 2015-2020.  He was a founding member of the Experts Group of the US-China Innovation Dialogue organized by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and China’s Ministry of Science & Technology (2008-2017).  In addition, he served as a special adviser on several cross-border innovation projects, including at the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office regarding intellectual property rights issues in China. He also has served as senior adviser on China and global affairs at several U.S. universities. From 1995-2000, he was general manager of Andersen Consulting in Beijing (now Accenture) and was founding president of Monitor Group China (2001-2002). He earned his PhD and MA from the University of California, Berkeley and his BA from the State University of New York.  

In 2006, he received the China National Friendship Award from then Premier Wen Jiabao in the Great Hall of the People in Beijing.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: OSIM Research Seminar Series - Dr. John Chen
description:
OSIM Research Seminar Series - Dr. John Chen

Alignment Structures and Ecosystem Performance: A Complexity-based Approach

Abstract:
A central strategy problem in ecosystems is the search for alignment – that is, how firms discover and converge upon technological choices that dictate how their interdependent activities will function together to realize complementarities and enable market success. Ecosystem alignment presents unique challenges due to its multilateral, non-vertical interdependencies. These complexities limit the effectiveness of traditional, dyadic alignment mechanisms. Conceptually, three fundamentally distinct search modes exist, each of which is commonly observed in practice: (a) through consensus (e.g., the WiFi standard); (b) by a single platform owner (e.g., iOS); and (c) de facto, where firms do not explicitly coordinate their search for alignment (e.g., some Smart TV systems). However, we know little about the relative efficacy of each of these modes, particularly with respect to the diverse structures of interdependence that we see in real-world ecosystems. Moreover, it is hard to find real-world counterfactuals to an observed alignment search mode and interdependence structure. Therefore, in this paper, we use computational modeling to contrast the efficacy of alignment across these modes. Our main insight is that the best search mode depends critically on the type of interdependence most prevalent in the ecosystem. When multilateral interdependence dominates, i.e., between the ecosystem’s alignment structure (i.e., the ecosystem’s “rules”) and firms, consensus-based alignment search achieves superior performance. When interdependence is primarily bilateral, i.e., between pairs of firms, the platform-owner mode outperforms the others. The de facto mode only prevails when interdependence is mostly unilateral, i.e., internal to firms.

name: Confident Aging — Frontiers of BrainHealth Lecture
description:

Friday, October 17 @ 12:00 p.m. CST

Confident Aging

Ian Robertson, PhD
Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin and Center for BrainHealth

Do you often find yourself thinking about getting older? Do you believe that aging inevitably means losing independence — or do you think it’s possible to maintain a rich, purposeful life as you grow older? Your outlook on aging matters more than you might think. Research shows that people with negative views about aging — starting as early as their fifties — tend to walk more slowly, socialize less, and experience a greater decline in cognitive abilities compared to those with a more positive and confident mindset.

Confidence plays a powerful role in how we age. It influences not just how we feel, but how we function. Neuroscience reveals that confidence boosts the brain in five key ways: it lifts mood, reduces anxiety, sharpens thinking, increases motivation, and enhances how others perceive us — making us more socially influential. Of course, we can’t pretend that aging doesn’t bring changes — our joints may be stiffer, hearing less sharp and reactions slower. But when we approach aging with confidence, these challenges are less likely to trigger morale-sapping feedback loops that lead to gradual withdrawal from new goals and experiences.

Renowned clinical psychologist Dr. Ian Robertson explores the beliefs and behaviors that shape our confidence, and how, within the limits of illness or circumstance, we can age more actively, happily, and with greater purpose. He is the T. Boone Pickens Distinguished Chair and co-leader of The BrainHealth Project at Center for BrainHealth and emeritus professor and co-director of the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin.

name: Computational Science Seminar by Dr. Preskella Mrad (The University of Texas at Dallas)
description:
Title: Parameter and State Space Reduction for Bayesian Inverse Problems with Application to Nonlinear Ice Sheet Flow Models Abstract: Solving large-scale Bayesian inverse problems often suffers from the twin computational challenges of high-dimensional input parameters and expensive forward models. This talk presents a framework for jointly reducing the parameter and state spaces to make these problems computationally tractable.To reduce the parameter dimension, we exploit problem-specific structure to construct a likelihood-informed subspace that efficiently captures the most significant updates from the prior to the posterior. To reduce the state dimension, we construct a reduced-order model using Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) to create a low-dimensional basis, complemented by the Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (DEIM) to efficiently evaluate the model's nonlinearities. 

We apply this joint reduction strategy to a Bayesian inversion problem involving a nonlinear ice sheet flow model described by the nonlinear Stokes equations. In this application, we infer the basal sliding coefficient using surface velocity observations. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, reducing the parameter space from 135 to 15 dimensions and the state space from 6,179 to just 15 dimensions. The results highlight the significant benefit of tailoring the state space reduction to the parameter-reduced posterior.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

description:

In the spirit of Whiskers and Paws, stop by and get a watercolor portrait of your favorite furry friend painted live by Caitlin McConnell. Bring a photo and watch as the magic unfolds or walk around and enjoy other activities while Caitlin paints your pet to perfection.


[ _____ ] Mirage Performance of Sonic Composition
1:00 p.m.
Gallery 5

Percussionists Drew Lang and Roland Muzquiz perform the graphic music notation designed by the artists Sara Dittrich and SV Randall, accompanying the video installation in the Crow’s New Media Gallery. Using the marimba and other percussive effect instruments, this experimental music score interprets visual and environmental data collected by the artists across areas of the Tularosa Basin in the southwestern United States—geographies historically associated with extreme atmospheric phenomena. Following the performance will be a Q&A with the artists.

Please note: The performance is 15 minutes long and will start promptly at 1:00 p.m. Space is limited. First come, first served.

Drew Lang has commissioned and premiered works for marimba in solo, chamber and concerto settings. He is a member of the Dallas Opera Orchestra, principal mallet player with the Dallas Wind Symphony and percussionist for Casa Mañana Musicals and Broadway Dallas. Lang is on the percussion faculties at Southern Methodist University and runs MARIMBA MADNESS summer percussion camp.

Roland Muzquiz is Percussion Director for Richardson High School. Along with this position, Mr. Muzquiz also serves as Principal Percussionist with the Dallas Wind Symphony and the East Texas Symphony Orchestra. He has also performed with the Dallas Opera, the Dallas Symphony Orchestra, the Plano Symphony Orchestra, the Richardson Symphony Orchestra, Texas Chamber Orchestra, Ft. Worth-Dallas Ballet, Ballet Arlington, Dallas Chamber Orchestra, Texas Wind Symphony, The Turtle Creek Chorale, and the San Antonio Symphony Orchestra.

Sara Dittrich is a Baltimore-based interdisciplinary artist. Her artworks include sculpture, prints, video, and interactive installations with biometric sensors, and data-driven performance. Often informed by residencies and travel, such projects have included time-lapse imaging of landscapes, local skies and tidal patterns, and the somatic effects of time and a place on the body. Dittrich’s work has been exhibited with venues such as the Baltimore Museum of Art, The Sculpture Center (Cleveland, OH), and DiverseWorks (Houston, TX).

SV Randall is an interdisciplinary artist, working with sculpture, installation, painting, and performance. Randall addresses the various ways in which objects mutate in nature and function across time. His work has been exhibited at venues such as David & Schweitzer Contemporary (Brooklyn, NY), the Richard and Dolly Maass Gallery (Purchase, NY), and the Villa Romana Palazzi di Casignana (Italy). He is currently an Assistant Professor of Visual and Performing Arts at the University of Texas at Dallas.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

Athenaeum hours: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday. Free admission.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: Mission 22: Suicide Prevention Awareness Challenge
description:
What is Mission 22?

 

Mission 22 is an annual fitness challenge with a critical purpose: to raise awareness for veteran suicide prevention. The event's name is a powerful nod to a 2013 statistic that highlighted a tragic reality—an average of 22 veterans die by suicide every single day. While more recent data indicates this number has slightly decreased to around 20, the event remains steadfast in its mission.

The challenge works to achieve several key goals:

Connect veterans with resources. They aim to link military-affiliated students with vital support services.

Fight mental health stereotypes. The event works to break down harmful stereotypes about mental health.

Support the transition to civilian life. It provides veterans with the tools they need for a successful and healthy life after service.

To honor the commitment and sacrifice of each branch of the military and to promote awareness, all students, staff, and faculty are invited to participate in one or more of the seven fitness challenges.

22 pushups for the Army22 squats for the Air Force22 pull-ups for the Marines22 jumping jacks for the Coast Guard22 sit-ups for the Navy22 cherry pickers for the Space Force22 modified or combination of exercise challenges for the general student body

name: The Impact of Cultural Differences in Causal Attributions on Discretionary Parole Decisions - Psychology Lecture Series
description:
Psychology Lecture Series

Title - The Impact of Cultural Differences in Causal Attributions on Discretionary Parole Decisions

Speaker: Amrita Telidevara
Doctoral Student, UT Dallas
Psychology

People from interdependent cultures, including Black, Hispanic, and East Asian Americans [vs. independent cultures, such as White Americans] view the self as connected to [vs. distinct from] the environment and, therefore, explain their behaviors using situational [vs. dispositional] attributions more. However, the U.S. justice system, shaped by White American cultural values, may expect parole candidates to explain their behaviors using dispositional [vs. situational] attributions, perceiving them as a sign of "accountability." In Study 1 (N = 765), White American mock parole commissioners, indeed, perceived parole candidates who provided dispositional [vs. situational] explanations as less likely to reoffend, and in Studies 2–3 (total N = 595), White American mock parole candidates provided more dispositional attributions, while mock minority candidates showed no such preference/favored situational explanations. In Study 4, by analyzing 183 real parole hearings via natural language processing methods, we found that candidates granted parole provided dispositional explanations more often. Together, these findings suggest that there may be a cultural mismatch between minority parole candidates and the expectations of the U.S. justice system, contributing to racial disparity in discretionary parole decisions.

This talk is in-person in JO 4.306.

Light snacks will be provided.

name: Digital Heritage Showcase with Michael Thomas. “Visualizing the Roman Villa: Virtual Preservation and Digital Archaeology at Oplontis"
description:
Please join us for the first talk of the O’Donnell Institute’s 2025/26 Digital Cultural Heritage lecture series featuring the work of UTD Faculty whose research overlaps with digital cultural heritage practices.

 

On Thursday, October 23, Edith O’Donnell Institute of Art History Director Michael Thomas will speak about digital heritage methods that have shaped the study and preservation of two ancient Roman sites: Oplontis Villa A, a monumental seaside residence, and “Villa” B, a commercial complex dedicated to wine storage and distribution. The lecture will detail the Oplontis Project’s use of 3D laser scanning, photogrammetry, GIS mapping, and a linked database to document the architectural remains and decorative programs of both sites. 

 

By combining preservation, accessibility, and interpretation, the Oplontis Project case study offers a model for how digital heritage can reframe our understanding of the environments in which ancient Romans lived and worked.

 

Michael L. Thomas is an Associate Provost and Director of the Edith O’Donnell Institute of Art History at the University of Texas at Dallas, where he also holds the Richard R. Brettell Distinguished University Chair. He also serves as the managing curator of the DMA Partnership at the UT Dallas Athenaeum. He has excavated in Italy for 30 years where he co-directs two projects: the ongoing Oplontis Project in Torre Annunziata and the Mugello Valley Archaeological Project which is now in publication phase. A collaborative and interdisciplinary project between UT Dallas and UT Austin, the Oplontis Project is a leader in the implementation and utilization of Digital Humanities. His publications include studies on an Etruscan architecture and archaeology, Roman art and architecture, Roman villas, Roman wine trade, and Roman numismatics.

name: Neuro-Adipo-Immune Axis of Chronic Primary Pain - Neuroscience Seminar Series
description:
Neuroscience Seminar Series

Title: Neuro-Adipo-Immune Axis of Chronic Primary Pain

Speaker:
Andrea Nackley, PhD
Duke University

This seminar will reveal new mechanisms of chronic primary pain conditions (CPPCs) in human and mouse. In landmark studies, our lab demonstrated that chronic primary pain is driven by catecholamine activation of adrenergic receptor beta-3 (Adrb3) on adipocytes. Activation of adipocyte Adrb3 1) stimulates release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and infiltration of immune cells in local tissues, 2) drives increased activity of primary afferent nociceptors in dorsal root ganglia, and 3) promotes neuroplastic changes in pain-relevant CNS structures. Further, activation of adipocyte Adrb3 modulates nociception and pain through epigenetic regulation of micro-RNAs. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of the adipo-neuro-immune axis in the development and resolution of CPPCs.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

description:
Callier FLASH Seminar in Speech, Language and Hearing

Title: Relationship Between Device Usage and Listening-Related Fatigue in Adults and Children With Cochlear Implants

Speaker: Swarali Joshi
PhD Student, UT Dallas

Cochlear implants (CIs) enable people with moderate-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss to perceive sounds, but perceptual outcomes with a CI remain highly variable from person-to-person. Individuals who wear their CI consistently tend to exhibit better auditory outcomes than those who do not wear their CI as often. However, even the best-performing CI users typically exert more effort to understand speech than their peers with normal hearing, which can lead to listening-related fatigue. In this study, we aimed to understand whether the amount of time an individual wears a CI each day influences their listening effort, listening-related fatigue, and subjective hearing abilities. We found that adults who do not wear their CIs consistently experience elevated levels of fatigue. We believe that this work provides valuable insights into how CI use influences quality of life beyond speech perception scores. The findings of the study will help guide clinicians in counseling patients to increase device usage to potentially reduce listening effort and associated listening fatigue, thereby improving the quality of life of those individuals.

Swarali is a doctoral student in Dr. Kelly Jahn’s Neuroaudiology Lab at UT Dallas. She earned her master’s degree in audiology from India. With clinical experience as an audiologist, she has worked in assessing and providing intervention for individuals with cochlear implants. Her research interests focus on factors that influence cochlear implant outcomes and the overall quality of life for CI users. She is particularly investigating how cochlear implant use impacts self-perceived listening-related fatigue, listening effort, and hearing abilities.

name: Computational Science Seminar by Dr. Gaik Ambartsoumian (The University of Texas at Arlington)
description:
Integral geometry and tomography along broken rays

Many conventional imaging modalities are based on information carried by electromagnetic or acoustic signals propagating along straight lines. Some typical examples include X-ray CT, optical tomography in the ballistic regime, imaging of fluid flows from acoustic transmission measurements, etc. The associated mathematical problems of image reconstruction require the study of transforms mapping an unknown image function (alternatively, a vector field or a symmetric tensor field) to a family of its integrals along straight lines. The list of such operators includes the (classical) Radon and X-ray transforms of scalar fields, Doppler (or longitudinal), transverse and mixed ray transforms of symmetric tensor fields, their momentum ray transforms of various orders, and others.

The mathematical models of the techniques described above ignore the scattered or reflected signals. However, it is well known that a sizeable portion of the measured signals falls into the latter category. Typically, the information carried by them is ignored or filtered out, essentially being treated as noise. This approach is not very efficient, and many researchers have been exploring creative ways to use that discarded data. One of the promising directions of such research is single scattering tomography, which leads to the study of generalizations along broken rays (or V-lines) of the transforms described above. In this talk, we will introduce many of these new transforms, discuss their properties, including kernel descriptions, injectivity and inversions, and illustrate the results with numerical simulations on smooth and non-smooth phantoms.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

Group topics may include adjustment, loneliness, academic/general stress, and relationships.
 

Process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

description:
Neuroscience Seminar Series

Title: Can You Feel the Rhythm? Circadian Rhythmicity as a Tool to Better Understand Pain and Nocicception

Speaker:
Nader Ghasemlou, PhD
Queen's University

Circadian (24-hour) rhythms govern most physiological systems. Using a translational approach, our research team has found that people with chronic low back pain experience pain in different ways: some have rhythmic pain while a majority are arrhythmic. This rhythmicity of pain is coupled with reduced opioid consumption and improved biopsychosocial outcomes, as well as immune cell activation patterns. In a preclinical model, we find that nociceptor-autonomous rhythms also play a role in pain sensitivity. The major goal of our research group is to characterize the mechanisms underlying these rhythms across cells and systems in the context of pain and neuroinflammation.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

We’ll start by loosening up our senses and getting to know each other through drawing. We’ll also watch a short BBC clip about prosopagnosia to think about perception and recognition in a playful way.

Activities:

Monica Steinberg is an Assistant Professor at the University of Hong Kong. Her research considers the intersection of art, fictional attribution, humor, and law. Recent publications include articles in American Art, Art History, Art Journal, Grey Room, and Crime, Media, Culture, as well as her forthcoming book, Lives of the Imaginary Artists in Cold War California (University of Chicago Press, 2025).

 

About the book:

If an artist is imaginary, whose self-expression is on display—and how can an imaginary artist paint a portrait or self-portrait? Lives of the Imaginary Artists explores how a group of real California artists created fictional counterparts. name: Moses Pendleton: PAREIDOLIA - A Photography Exhibit
description:
Join us for a special evening celebrating the visionary artistry of MOMIX's founder Moses Pendleton. The event begins with an intimate artist talk at the ATC LED Wall, where he will share insights into his creative world. Following the conversation, guests are invited to a reception in the ATC Lecture Hall Lobby and a viewing of the photography exhibition in the ATC Exhibition Hall.

Best known for his surreal movement language onstage, Moses Pendleton now turns his eye to stillness. PAREIDOLIA is a photographic meditation on impermanence — featuring decomposing irises, aging sunflowers, dried cabbage heads, corn husks, tree stumps, and frozen puddles caught mid-thaw. What at first glance appears to be botanical detritus slowly reveals something else: a figure, a mask, a spirit — unexpected beauty rising from organic ruin.

Through the lens of pareidolia — the psychological phenomenon where we perceive patterns or faces in randomness — these images do not simply document decay; they elevate it. The broken becomes sculptural, the spoiled becomes sublime. PAREIDOLIA invites us to see not just what is dying, but what is becoming — in all its strange and haunting grace.

“There is choreography in the cracks,” says Pendleton. “A slow dance in the decay.”

About MOMIX:

Recognized internationally for its exceptional innovation and physical artistry, MOMIX is a company of dancer-illusionists under the direction of Moses Pendleton. Blending illusion, beauty, magic, fun, and inventiveness, MOMIX presents a collection of iconic pieces from its illustrious repertoire. Surreal, wondrous, and massively creative—there’s nothing like MOMIX!

About the Richard Brettell Award in the Arts:

The Brettell Award is the highest honor given to artists by the University of Texas at Dallas. It shines the spotlight on luminaries working in any area on the broad spectrum of artistic endeavors, including the visual arts, music, literature, performance, and architecture/design. By highlighting artistic excellence, the award recognizes and advances the essential and fundamental role of the arts in the life of the university.

name: The Jean & Bill Booziotis Distinguished Lecture
description:
The Jean & Bill Booziotis Distinguished Lecture Series presents Dr. Breatriz Luna, PhD, from the University of Pittsburgh, Department of Psychiatry: 

Why teen brain development and teens unpredictable behaviors are so important to forming adulthood

We often think of the teen years as tumultuous, and from the perspective of parents or adults, they can be difficult to navigate. Teens at times may act like adults, yet at other times, they make unreasonable risky choices that leaves us baffled, often leading to conflict. However, brain development studies now show that these behavioral changes are critical for them to form into adaptive adults. For more than 20 years, we have been studying how the adolescent brain functions determining adulthood. Dr. Beatriz Luna will present her latest findings showing that brain chemicals that support reward behaviors change in specific ways during this time, helping us understand why teens can be impulsive and risk takers—and offering insight into why many mental illnesses emerge at this period. We have also found new evidence that the critical thinking parts of the teen brain are highly plastic. This helps us understand and appreciate the importance of the range of experiences—whether adaptive or risky behaviors—that teens gravitate toward. These experiences play a crucial role in forming the adult brain and preparing it for aging. In sum, the unpredictability of the teenage brain is a great and important part of brain development. Understanding the underlying brain mechanisms at this stage of development can inform approaches to support a healthier, more adaptive adulthood.


REGISTER 

Registration if FREE, but required.
 

Background: Dr. Luna is Distinguished Professor of Psychiatry, Bioengineering, Pyschology and Radiology, and Staunton Professor of Pediatrics and Psychiatry at the University of Pittsburgh.  Dr. Luna’s research uses multimodal neuroimaging methods including: functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI), Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), Magnetoencephalography (MEG), Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI). Her findings have led to influential developmental models emphasizing the implications of specialization of different brain systems with regards to cognitive development.

About the event: This event is part of the Center for Vital Longevity's Jean & Bill Booziotis Distinguished Lecture Series, made possible by the late Bill Booziotis, former president of Booziotis and Company Architects and Center for Vital Longevity Advisory Council Member. Bill Booziotis and his wife, Jean, established the series to bring the Center’s work, focused on understanding the science of the aging mind, to the public

name: Examining Ultrasonic Vocalizations in Rat Models of Communication Disorder Models - Neuroscience Seminar Series - First Year Presentation
description:
Neuroscience Seminar Series - First Year Presentation

Title: Examining Ultrasonic Vocalizations in Rat Models of Communication Disorder Models

Speaker:
Samantha Kroon
Student, UT Dallas

Communication disorders significantly impair social connection, emotional expression, and access to healthcare. Rats produce ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) which can be used as a translational readout for studying communication deficits and their recovery. This study models two such conditions in rats: (1) recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (RLNi), which causes vocal fold paralysis and limits voice production, and (2) Rett Syndrome (RTT), a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired speech and language production, in addition to social difficulties associated with autism spectrum disorders. Motor and social deficits as marked through USV acoustics features and reduced call rate were seen in both RLNi and RTT rats. Future work aims to target these deficits with the use of vagal nerve stimulation paired with a swallowing task to rehabilitate motor dysfunction in the larynx.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

description:
Register for free ↗

Friday, November 7 @ 12:00 p.m. CST

Visualizing Molecular Events in the Brain with Hemogenetic MRI

Nan Li, PhD
UTSW Advanced Imaging Research Center and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Brain Institute

The brain’s extensive vascular network enables hemodynamic imaging to serve not only as a readout of general brain activity (conventional BOLD fMRI), but also — when combined with synthetic biology — as a potent reporter for molecular signaling. We developed hemogenetic MRI, a novel approach that enables the translation of molecular signaling events in the brain into spatially localized, hemodynamic MRI signals through the use of genetically encoded reporters. In this talk, Dr. Nan Li introduces hemogenetic MRI tools designed to probe brain function at cell-type and subcellular resolution. Read more.

description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: Fall 2025 "Signature Required" Period to Withdraw from UG Courses 2nd 8-Week Session
Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.
