name: Mystical Arts of Tibet: Mandala Sand Painting
description:
Tuesday, November 11 - Friday, November 14, 11am-5pm

Tibetan Buddhist Monks from the Drepung Loseling Monastery return to the Crow Museum on the campus of UT Dallas for a week-long residency to construct a magnificent Tantric Buddhist mandala sand painting. Using traditional metal funnels called chak-pur, millions of grains of crushed marble are painstakingly laid into place in this ancient spiritual art form to generate energies for global healing.

Throughout the week, visitors are invited to stop by and observe this sacred practice, witness the mandala’s intricate evolution, and reflect on the themes of compassion, impermanence, and the interconnectedness of all life.

As the monks from Drepung Loseling Monastery create a traditional mandala nearby, visitors of all ages are invited to take part in a hands-on Community Sand Painting experience. This collaborative experience offers a unique opportunity to explore the meditative and creative practice of sand painting while expressing ideas that resonate with our own community. Whether you're a student, a family, or simply curious, this is a chance to connect and reflect on the themes of the mandala—impermanence, mindfulness, and shared purpose.

Community Sand Painting Contest
UT Dallas students are invited to submit an original design for this year’s Community Sand Painting, which will be brought to life by visitors throughout the week-long Mystical Arts of Tibet residency. The design should reflect the spirit and creativity of the UT Dallas Comet community while also drawing inspiration from traditional Tibetan mandala design principles, such as balance, symmetry, and symbolic representation of harmony and interconnectedness.

The contest winner will be contacted the week of November 3 and will be expected to sketch their design onto the 3x3’ sand painting base on Monday, November 10 between the hours of 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. The winner will receive a Crow Museum goodie bag filled with museum merchandise and surprises. 

DEADLINE: 5:00 p.m., Monday, October 27, 2025

name: Artistic exchange and community building at a studio-turned-museum: The Elisabet Ney Museum’s Engagement in the 21st century
description:
Keeping true to its original mission and the historicity of the location and collection- the staff of the Elisabet Ney Museum, artists and researchers continue to navigate the challenges of producing engaging events and effectual curatorial programming. With this panel, researchers, museum staff, and local artists consider the trajectories of influence and significance that the Elisabet Ney Museum has to offer as Texas’ first artist studio into the 21st century.

PANEL SPEAKERS

Jacquelyn Delin McDonald

Dr. Jacquelyn Delin McDonald is an art historian whose research focuses on art and its historicity from German-speaking countries, sculptural types, American art, and women artists during the long nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Her current book project involves the study of German-American sculptor Elisabet Ney. She has published on Ney as well as the ‘sculptress phenomenon’ of the late-nineteenth century. She is currently a Lecturer at the University of Texas at Dallas, as well as an adjunct faculty member at Texas Christian University, and the University of North Texas. She also assists the Elisabet Ney Museum as a research consultant when the opportunity arises! She has held fellowships with the U.S. Capitol as well as the Edith O’Donnell Institute of Art History. 

Lindsay Barras

Lindsay, originally from Houston, has been at the Ney for 17 years, starting as a Gallery Attendant. After receiving a BFA from the Kansas City Art Institute, she worked in the arts sector in London and San Francisco. She received her Master’s Degree in Art Education from UT Austin with a focus in Museum Education. She has experience developing programs that center around visual literacy and portraiture as well as planning large-scale community events. She’s a vital part of the museum’s engagement efforts, effectively serving as the museum’s Education Coordinator. 

Jade Walker

Jade Walker is a sculptor and an active member of the arts community living in Austin, Texas. She received her BFA from the University of Florida and her MFA from the University of Texas at Austin. Walker held the position of Executive Director at the Visual Arts Center in the Department of Art and Art History at the University of Texas for over a decade. She also served as Director of Austin Art Alliance Austin and held the position of studio manager for artist Deborah Roberts. In the past, she participated in the City of Austin’s Art in Public Places as a panel member as well as steering committee member for The Art Galleries at Black Studies at The University of Texas.  She currently serves on the board of Austin Art Alliance and Fusebox. Since 2022, she has led the Elisabet Ney Museum as Director and Curator, managing the museum and historic grounds as well as moving the museum through a new interpretive plan with MuseWork, large capital improvement project with the City of Austin, and a rehabilitation plan for the landscape with Catherine O’Connor and Ten Eyck Landscape Architects. 

Renee Lai

Renee Lai is an Asian American artist working in painting and drawing. Her latest body of work explores the self in relation to boundaries in the landscape. Lai draws on her longstanding interest in landscape to help her shape her compositions and to understand our relationship to the world. Lai graduated with her MFA in Studio Art: Painting and Drawing from the University of Texas at Austin in 2019. Lai has an undergraduate degree in English and Studio Art with Honors from Dartmouth College, and she also studied painting at the New York Studio School. Lai has been an artist in residence at Vermont Studio Center, the Line hotel (Texas), and Monson Arts Center (Maine). Lai has exhibited nationally and internationally, most recently with solo shows at the Elisabet Ney Museum and GrayDuck Gallery. 

Rosa Nussbaum

Rosa Nussbaum is a visual artist who works at the intersection of performance and sculpture with an emphasis on interactivity and digital technologies. Their work speculates on queer, feminist alternatives to the systems of power under which we live. In their work, they use storytelling and humour to make difficult topics approachable. 

Rosa had exhibited internationally including showing work with Residency Unlimited New York, the Hiroshima MoCA and Glasgow International. Their most recent exhibition Housewives of the Queer Hearth is an interactive media installation exploring a speculative vision of queer feminist architecture and urban planning, in collaboration with fellow artist Kevin Brophy, showcasing the work of other queer and gender non-conforming artists.

They are currently a PhD candidate at the University of Melbourne, Australia and hold an MFA in Studio Art: Transmedia from the University of Austin at Texas.

name: Mystical Arts of Tibet: Mandala Sand Painting
description:

Tibetan Buddhist Monks from the Drepung Loseling Monastery return to the Crow Museum on the campus of UT Dallas for a week-long residency to construct a magnificent Tantric Buddhist mandala sand painting. Using traditional metal funnels called chak-pur, millions of grains of crushed marble are painstakingly laid into place in this ancient spiritual art form to generate energies for global healing.

Throughout the week, visitors are invited to stop by and observe this sacred practice, witness the mandala’s intricate evolution, and reflect on the themes of compassion, impermanence, and the interconnectedness of all life.

As the monks from Drepung Loseling Monastery create a traditional mandala nearby, visitors of all ages are invited to take part in a hands-on Community Sand Painting experience. This collaborative experience offers a unique opportunity to explore the meditative and creative practice of sand painting while expressing ideas that resonate with our own community. Whether you're a student, a family, or simply curious, this is a chance to connect and reflect on the themes of the mandala—impermanence, mindfulness, and shared purpose.

UT Dallas students are invited to submit an original design for this year’s Community Sand Painting, which will be brought to life by visitors throughout the week-long Mystical Arts of Tibet residency. The design should reflect the spirit and creativity of the UT Dallas Comet community while also drawing inspiration from traditional Tibetan mandala design principles, such as balance, symmetry, and symbolic representation of harmony and interconnectedness.

The contest winner will be contacted the week of November 3 and will be expected to sketch their design onto the 3x3’ sand painting base on Monday, November 10 between the hours of 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. The winner will receive a Crow Museum goodie bag filled with museum merchandise and surprises.

name: Artistic exchange and community building at a studio-turned-museum: The Elisabet Ney Museum’s Engagement in the 21st century
description:
Keeping true to its original mission and the historicity of the location and collection- the staff of the Elisabet Ney Museum, artists and researchers continue to navigate the challenges of producing engaging events and effectual curatorial programming. With this panel, researchers, museum staff, and local artists consider the trajectories of influence and significance that the Elisabet Ney Museum has to offer as Texas’ first artist studio into the 21st century.

PANEL SPEAKERS

Jacquelyn Delin McDonald

Dr. Jacquelyn Delin McDonald is an art historian whose research focuses on art and its historicity from German-speaking countries, sculptural types, American art, and women artists during the long nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Her current book project involves the study of German-American sculptor Elisabet Ney. She has published on Ney as well as the ‘sculptress phenomenon’ of the late-nineteenth century. She is currently a Lecturer at the University of Texas at Dallas, as well as an adjunct faculty member at Texas Christian University, and the University of North Texas. She also assists the Elisabet Ney Museum as a research consultant when the opportunity arises! She has held fellowships with the U.S. Capitol as well as the Edith O’Donnell Institute of Art History. 

Lindsay Barras

Lindsay, originally from Houston, has been at the Ney for 17 years, starting as a Gallery Attendant. After receiving a BFA from the Kansas City Art Institute, she worked in the arts sector in London and San Francisco. She received her Master’s Degree in Art Education from UT Austin with a focus in Museum Education. She has experience developing programs that center around visual literacy and portraiture as well as planning large-scale community events. She’s a vital part of the museum’s engagement efforts, effectively serving as the museum’s Education Coordinator. 

Jade Walker

Jade Walker is a sculptor and an active member of the arts community living in Austin, Texas. She received her BFA from the University of Florida and her MFA from the University of Texas at Austin. Walker held the position of Executive Director at the Visual Arts Center in the Department of Art and Art History at the University of Texas for over a decade. She also served as Director of Austin Art Alliance Austin and held the position of studio manager for artist Deborah Roberts. In the past, she participated in the City of Austin’s Art in Public Places as a panel member as well as steering committee member for The Art Galleries at Black Studies at The University of Texas.  She currently serves on the board of Austin Art Alliance and Fusebox. Since 2022, she has led the Elisabet Ney Museum as Director and Curator, managing the museum and historic grounds as well as moving the museum through a new interpretive plan with MuseWork, large capital improvement project with the City of Austin, and a rehabilitation plan for the landscape with Catherine O’Connor and Ten Eyck Landscape Architects. 

Renee Lai

Renee Lai is an Asian American artist working in painting and drawing. Her latest body of work explores the self in relation to boundaries in the landscape. Lai draws on her longstanding interest in landscape to help her shape her compositions and to understand our relationship to the world. Lai graduated with her MFA in Studio Art: Painting and Drawing from the University of Texas at Austin in 2019. Lai has an undergraduate degree in English and Studio Art with Honors from Dartmouth College, and she also studied painting at the New York Studio School. Lai has been an artist in residence at Vermont Studio Center, the Line hotel (Texas), and Monson Arts Center (Maine). Lai has exhibited nationally and internationally, most recently with solo shows at the Elisabet Ney Museum and GrayDuck Gallery. 

Rosa Nussbaum

Rosa Nussbaum is a visual artist who works at the intersection of performance and sculpture with an emphasis on interactivity and digital technologies. Their work speculates on queer, feminist alternatives to the systems of power under which we live. In their work, they use storytelling and humour to make difficult topics approachable. 

Rosa had exhibited internationally including showing work with Residency Unlimited New York, the Hiroshima MoCA and Glasgow International. Their most recent exhibition Housewives of the Queer Hearth is an interactive media installation exploring a speculative vision of queer feminist architecture and urban planning, in collaboration with fellow artist Kevin Brophy, showcasing the work of other queer and gender non-conforming artists.

They are currently a PhD candidate at the University of Melbourne, Australia and hold an MFA in Studio Art: Transmedia from the University of Austin at Texas.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: Fall 2025 "Signature Required" Period to Withdraw from UG Courses 2nd 8-Week Session
Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: DBT-U (Dialectical Behavioral Therapy for University Students)
description:
DBT-U is an open, eight-week, hybrid process- and skills-based group for students to learn and develop coping skills and strategies to improve individual functioning. This group is specifically for clients who have difficulties in emotion regulation, interpersonal difficulties, and pattern of crisis. Group members learn topics related to mindfulness skills, interpersonal effectiveness and communication strategies, emotion regulation, and distress tolerance skills in a structured and supportive learning environment. Each group consists of a brief mindfulness exercise, check-in/introductions, introduction of new skills, discussion/experiential practice and assignment of practice exercise and check-out.
 

Hybrid skills/process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Hybrid skills/process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day, though new skills and strategies are often a topic of discussion. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For Hybrid skills/process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

If you are a current or recent client, reach out to our Groups & Workshops Coordinator at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to schedule a screening meeting.

Jonathan Rosand, MD, MSc
Henry and Allison McCance Center for Brain Health and Center for Neurotechnology and Neurorecovery (CNTR)

The Global Brain Care Coalition (GBCC) is an international learning health care system grounded in providing people with the knowledge and tools to take action in caring for their brains — its mission is to make proactive, evidence-based brain care simple and accessible to communities worldwide to promote brain health and prevent disease. description:
Level Up Your Cloud & AI Skills with AWS

The University of Texas at Dallas is partnering with the AWS Skills Center to offer a dynamic virtual learning series designed to help you become a certified Cloud and AI Practitioner. This exclusive cohort-based program runs from September 12 to December 5, 2025, with weekly Friday sessions (excluding Thanksgiving week).

Learn more about the entire series and all registration information.

 

 Register for Becoming an AI Practitioner Part 5 

 

Date: Friday, November 21, 2025Time: 3:00–6:30 PM CSTTopic: Implementing Generative AIDescription: In this session, students will learn about security, governance, and compliance considerations for AI systems on AWS. Key topics include implementing a defense-in-depth security approach, using AWS services like IAM, KMS, and CloudWatch to secure AI workloads, applying governance frameworks and controls, and meeting compliance requirements for AI applications. name: The Wellness Lab
description:
Saturdays, September 6-December 6 2025

Edith and Peter O'Donnell Athenaeum
777 Loop Rd SW, Richardson, TX 75080

 

The Wellness Lab is a place for everyone wanting to try something new. This well being retreat inside of the Crow Museum of Asian Art at UT Dallas offers explorations in mindfulness, yoga, ayurveda, well being and art. Self-compassion begins with taking time to explore silence, awareness, togetherness and understanding. These classes are for you.  

Why Join the Wellness Lab?

Because college is a lot. And your nervous system needs rest, too. 

Learn practical tools to manage anxiety and overwhelmBuild a habit of self-awareness and mental clarityConnect with a peaceful community of peersBegin your weekend with presence and intention
Please note: Each series requires separate registration for each date.
 

The Mindful Hour  

9 am - 9: 45 am

$20 Public  $0 UTD Staff, Faculty, students$0 Museum membersStart your Saturday in stillness. Join us inside the tranquil Crow Museum for guided mindfulness, grounding breathwork, and simple centering techniques that build resilience and reduce stress. 

Whether you’re new to meditation or already have a practice, this space is for everyone — especially students who want to feel more calm, clear, and connected. 

Come as you are. No mats, apps, or experience required — just your breath. 

Reserve your spot at the link below. Please ensure you select your preferred date. 

Register

 

The Yoga Hour: Gentle/Restorative/Vinyasa/Yin  

10 am - 10:45 am  

$20 Public  $0 UTD Staff, Faculty, students$0 Museum membersJoin us for Yoga in the Art Museum led by talented and certified yoga instructors in the community. All levels welcome!  

Reserve your spot at the link below. Please ensure you select your preferred date. 

Register

 

The Everything Hour:  

11 am - 1 pm

$20 Public  $0 UTD Staff, Faculty, students$0 Museum membersArt, Sound and Relaxation fill the Everything Hour with experiences in the open art studio, sound bath and programs on well being and self-compassion. See the schedule below.

September 6, 11 am - 1 pm: Lego Printmaking Workshop

Learn how to make art with legos! Join Dallas artist Leili Arai Tavallaei (@at_leili) for a 2 hour workshop on lego printmaking. You’ll get to create your very own print and learn accessible printmaking techniques. Come hang out, play with legos, and create with us. (Art supplies will be provided.)


September 13, 11am-1pm: Exquisite Hunt Workshop

Explore the museum in this sketchbook scavenger hunt! Join Dallas artist Leili Arai Tavallaei (@at_leili) for a 2 hour workshop on drawing the world around us. You’ll get to discover a new side of the Crow Museum and learn drawing techniques. We encourage you to bring a sketchbook and your curiosity. (Additional art supplies will be provided.)


September 20: Sensory Drawing

We’ll start by loosening up our senses and getting to know each other through drawing. Participants will explore blind contour drawing and drawing by touch, inspired by Carlotta’s practice of sensory art. We’ll also watch a short BBC clip about prosopagnosia to think about perception and recognition in a playful way.

Activities:

• Create a series of 5 small drawings using extremely limited sensory information (drawing with closed eyes, by touch, or without looking at the page).

• After a short break, we’ll experiment with color using jelly pads and acrylic paint to make prints based on sensory drawings.
 

September 27: Collage / Abstract Fall Fruits

Fall brings abundance—and collage is the perfect way to celebrate it. We’ll cut, layer, and combine everyday images of fruit, nature, kitchens, and seasonal decorations into abstract compositions.

Activities:

• Plan and layer cut-out images into a single abstract collage.

• Focus on visual balance and rhythm while letting intuition lead.

• Play with combining many fragments into one whole artwork.

 

October 4, 11 am - 1 pm: Shape Chasing Workshop/Exquisite Hunt Workshop (outdoors, weather permitting)

Come paint outside with us! Join Dallas artist Leili Arai Tavallaei (@at_leili) for a 2 hour workshop on painting the world en plein air (in the outdoors). You’ll get to create your very own painting and learn about outdoor painting techniques. Enjoy the Texas sunshine and create with us. (Art supplies will be provided.)
 

October 25, 11 am – 1 pm: Sleep Sessions

Ever wonder what really happens when you sleep—and why it matters so much? Join us for a friendly and engaging look at how good sleep helps your body, brain, and mood thrive. We’ll explore what the different stages of sleep do for your health, and share simple, practical tips to help you sleep better and feel more refreshed.
 

November 1, 11 am – 1 pm: Sleep Sessions

Ever wonder what really happens when you sleep—and why it matters so much? Join us for a friendly and engaging look at how good sleep helps your body, brain, and mood thrive. We’ll explore what the different stages of sleep do for your health, and share simple, practical tips to help you sleep better and feel more refreshed.
 

November 8: Halloween Fun / Shadows & Prints

We’ll celebrate the spirit of Halloween with a playful still-life setup. Pumpkins, fruits, and spooky objects will be arranged under a dramatic light source. First, we’ll draw from observation, then shift to printmaking to capture the spirit of the season.

Activities:

• Set up a Halloween-inspired still life with a single strong light source to create shadows.

• Draw the composition with expressive lines.

• Experiment with jelly pad printmaking using acrylic paint.
 

November 15: Group Project / Botanical Drawing

We’ll close the workshop with a large-scale collaborative art-science drawing. Inspired by the natural world, participants will bring their own images of plants, leaves, and neighborhood animals or insects. Together, we’ll create a shared artwork on a roll of paper that combines drawing, text, and mixed materials.

Activities:

• Begin with short reflections: What do you notice in quiet moments? What small details catch your attention in your surroundings?

• Each participant contributes drawings, words, and colors to a shared roll of paper.

• The final piece will be a layered, collaborative landscape of the group’s collective imagination.

name: Anxiety Toolbox Skills & Support Drop-In #2 (NEW!)
description:
An ongoing supportive space designed for people struggling with a variety of anxiety-related concerns. Looking for a flexible space to talk through your worries, connect with others, and learn tools for managing anxiety? Join us for Anxiety Toolbox: Skills and Support, a weekly space where you can share what’s on your mind, find encouragement, and learn strategies to cope with anxious thoughts and stress. Most weeks focus on open support and connection; once a month, we feature a mini-skills workshop on practical tools like calming your nervous system, managing racing thoughts, and finding balance. Come as you are, stay as long as you like — no registration required.
 

To join, simply click the Comet Calendar link at the start time. If you’d like reminders and an easier check-in, you can also message us at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to be added to the roster.

These groups provide an opportunity for support from others who hold similar identities or life experiences. Participation is open and drop-in style, meaning members do not have to be current clients of the Student Counseling Center, and you may attend meetings as often or as seldom as you like. Support groups are open to all UTD students, and no group screening is required. Please note support groups are not the same as therapy groups in that they are more focused on building community and peer support guided by one of our therapists than in-depth therapeutic intervention.

Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

11 am - 1 pm

$20 Public  $0 UTD Staff, Faculty, students$0 Museum membersArt, Sound and Relaxation fill the Everything Hour with experiences in the open art studio, sound bath and programs on well being and self-compassion. See the schedule below.

September 6, 11 am - 1 pm: Lego Printmaking Workshop

Learn how to make art with legos! Join Dallas artist Leili Arai Tavallaei (@at_leili) for a 2 hour workshop on lego printmaking. September 13, 11am-1pm: Exquisite Hunt Workshop

Explore the museum in this sketchbook scavenger hunt! Join Dallas artist Leili Arai Tavallaei (@at_leili) for a 2 hour workshop on drawing the world around us. You’ll get to discover a new side of the Crow Museum and learn drawing techniques. We encourage you to bring a sketchbook and your curiosity. (Additional art supplies will be provided.)


September 20: Sensory Drawing

We’ll start by loosening up our senses and getting to know each other through drawing. Participants will explore blind contour drawing and drawing by touch, inspired by Carlotta’s practice of sensory art. We’ll also watch a short BBC clip about prosopagnosia to think about perception and recognition in a playful way.

Activities:

• Create a series of 5 small drawings using extremely limited sensory information (drawing with closed eyes, by touch, or without looking at the page).

• After a short break, we’ll experiment with color using jelly pads and acrylic paint to make prints based on sensory drawings.

Fall brings abundance—and collage is the perfect way to celebrate it. We’ll cut, layer, and combine everyday images of fruit, nature, kitchens, and seasonal decorations into abstract compositions.

Activities:

• Plan and layer cut-out images into a single abstract collage.

• Focus on visual balance and rhythm while letting intuition lead.

• Play with combining many fragments into one whole artwork.

description:
Neuroscience Seminar Series - First Year Presentation

Title: Molecular Changes in the Basolateral Amygdala Following Vagus Nerve Stimulation-Enhanced Extinction of Conditioned Fear

Speaker:
Yara El Zoghby
Student, UT Dallas

Fear is an evolutionary conserved emotional state essential for survival, but dysfunction in this system gives rise to multiple psychopathological disorders including posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Patients suffering from PTSD resist extinction of the fear response, limiting the effectiveness of exposure-based therapies. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) accelerates the extinction of conditioned fear in male rats by inducing plasticity in the infralimbic-basolateral amygdala (IL-BLA) pathway, and decreasing activity regulated cytoskeletal-associated protein (Arc) protein levels in the BLA. Here, we replicated previous findings by showing that VNS at 0.4mA intensity, 500µs pulse width (PW) and 30Hz frequency, enhances extinction learning in male rats and investigated whether similar VNS parameters would result in enhanced extinction learning in female rats. Basolateral amygdala (BLA) tissues were collected for downstream proteomic analysis to better understand the molecular drivers of VNS-enhanced extinction effects.

name: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

name: Digital Heritage Showcase with Anne Balsamo. “Public Memory:  The AIDS Memorial Quilt Interactive Project"
description:
The AIDS Quilt Touch is 25-year project of digital cultural heritage to ensure future access and record of the cultural history of a fragile historical monument.  This presentation shows work from the Narrative Threads exhibition, and a real-time demonstration of the Virtual Quilt Browser.

Dr. Anne Balsamo is the Director of IQ Design at UT Dallas and a Distinguished University Professor in the School of Arts, Humanities, and Technology at UTD.  Her current research interests include digital cultural heritage, media archeology, and speculative design.  As a full professor in the AHT, she teaches courses in Technoculture, Digital Cultural Heritage, and Media Studies.  She has been a leader in the field of digital humanities nationally, serving on the Advisory Board of HASTAC (Humanities, Arts, Science, and Technology Advanced Co-laboratory) since its founding in 2003.  In 2011, she published the work, Designing Culture: The Technological Imagination at Work, a transmedia book that elaborates a reproductive theory of technology and culture through examples of her public interactive projects.  Since 2001, she has worked with a distributed team of creative technologists to build AIDS Quilt Touch, a web-based interactive browser for the AIDS Memorial Quilt.

name: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

Athenaeum hours: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday. Free admission.

name: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: The Role of the Lateral Entorhinal Cortex in Cocaine Seeking - Neuroscience Seminar Series - First Year Presentation
description:
Neuroscience Seminar Series - First Year Presentation

Title: The Role of the Lateral Entorhinal Cortex in Cocaine Seeking

Speaker:
Leila Mousavi
Student, UT Dallas

Drug-associated memories triggered by environmental cues are a major driver of relapse in cocaine use disorder. The lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) projects to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and may contribute to cue-driven drug seeking, but this circuit has not been well studied. We first attempted to record neural activity from LEC projections to the NAc using a retrograde GCaMP method with fiber photometry, but this did not produce reliable calcium signals during cocaine self-administration. Therefore, we used a broader approach by injecting pAAV.CAG.GCaMP6f directly into the LEC and tested animals in a food self-administration setup. We recorded calcium-dependent activity on the final day of food self-administration, the first and final day of extinction, and reinstatement. The behavioral results showed that animals learned to self-administer food, responded less during extinction, and responded more when exposed to cues. Fiber photometry showed that LEC activity was higher in the calcium-dependent channel (465 nm) compared to the isosbestic channel (415 nm), which shows neural activity detection. However, these results are limited by the small number of animals and off-target viral spread. In future work, we plan to use both methods in the cocaine self-administration model to see if LEC–NAc neurons are active during cue-induced drug seeking.

description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: Tracking the Aberrant Biochemistry in Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM) and Neuroblastoma (NB) Using Nuclear Magnetic Resonance - Neuroscience Seminar Series - First Year Presentation
description:
Neuroscience Seminar Series - First Year Presentation

Title: Tracking the Aberrant Biochemistry in Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM) and Neuroblastoma (NB) Using Nuclear Magnetic Resonance

Speaker:
Fiyinfoluwa Edun
Student, UT Dallas

Glioblastoma and neuroblastoma are highly aggressive cancers with poor prognosis, driven by a profound yet incompletely understood metabolic dysregulation. Using NMR spectroscopy and ¹³C-tracer analysis, we mapped the metabolic networks in these cancers, focusing on glucose, branched-chain amino acid (BCAA), and choline metabolism. We discovered that both cancers rapidly consume the leucine derivative α-ketoisocaproate (KIC), which serves as an anaplerotic substrate to replenish the TCA cycle or is recycled back to leucine. Both cell lines exhibited a strong Warburg effect, with neuroblastoma displaying a particularly aggressive glycolytic phenotype. The main goal of this study is to identify potential ¹³C metabolic biomarkers for the aberrant biochemical activities in glioblastoma and neuroblastoma via ¹³C NMR spectroscopy.

name: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

The Graduate Student Assembly (GSA) is the representative governing body of graduate students at UT Dallas. description:
The Student Wellness Center and Office of Human Subjects Protections invite you to attend the Comet Voice Suicide Prevention Training for Human Subjects Protections. You will learn the SAFER model for intervention, a structured approach designed to facilitate meaningful conversations and provide support to individuals in crisis. By the end of this training, you will be better prepared to engage with and support individuals at risk, contributing to a community that prioritizes mental health and well-being.

name: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: The Early Edge: Essentials for Growing Minds
description:
Parenting isn’t one-size-fits-all—and we’re here to support your unique journey. Join our dynamic new series where University experts team up with real parents to explore science-based strategies for the challenges you face every day. From picky eating and screen time battles to nurturing your mental health and your child’s curiosity, we’ll cover it all. Designed for parents of children ages 0 to 10, each session blends expert insights with small group discussions so you’ll leave feeling informed, empowered, and connected. Children are welcome to attend and engage in activities with our college students.

$15 per session or $90 for the series. Snacks and drinks, including wine, included! Register to attend at https://alumni.utdallas.edu/connect/events/view/?entry=3698

“Feeding Kids Without Frustration”

Tired of negotiating every bite or worrying if your child is getting what they need? In this session, we’ll tackle the everyday stress of mealtime and share practical, science-based strategies for make healthy eating more achievable—and less of a power struggle.

name: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: Comet Voice Suicide Prevention Training for Human Subjects Protections - Fall 2025/Spring 2026
description:
The Student Wellness Center and Office of Human Subjects Protections invite you to attend the Comet Voice Suicide Prevention Training for Human Subjects Protections. This training aims to equip attendees with essential knowledge and skills to effectively identify and respond to individuals at risk of suicide. You will learn the SAFER model for intervention, a structured approach designed to facilitate meaningful conversations and provide support to individuals in crisis. This model emphasizes understanding risk factors and warning signs of someone experiencing suicide ideation. By the end of this training, you will be better prepared to engage with and support individuals at risk, contributing to a community that prioritizes mental health and well-being.

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

The Student Wellness Center and Office of Human Subjects Protections invite you to attend the Comet Voice Suicide Prevention Training for Human Subjects Protections. By the end of this training, you will be better prepared to engage with and support individuals at risk, contributing to a community that prioritizes mental health and well-being.

name: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

name: Graduate Student Assembly General Body Business Meeting
description:
The Graduate Student Assembly (GSA) is the representative governing body of graduate students at UT Dallas. GSA constitutes leaders elected by graduate students each year and consists of an executive team and school representatives, as well as appointed students on the judicial board, the events team, and the marketing team. 

GSA holds monthly business meetings to discuss important issues affecting graduate students and vote on proposed solutions and targeted events to meet graduate students' needs. GSA welcomes all members of the UT Dallas community to attend meetings and provides an open forum opportunity for non-leadership members to address GSA. Please join us!

Ladysmith Black Mambazo
description:
Ladysmith Black Mambazo, formed by Joseph Shabalala in 1960, is a Grammy-winning South African male choral group performing in traditional isicathamiya and mbube vocal styles. They gained international fame after collaborating with Paul Simon on his 1986 "Graceland" album and have ince become cultural ambassadors of South African heritage through their prolific musical career. 

Parking Information:



Use Google Maps to drive to Parking Structure 1 (PS1) and park in a space with a Gold or Orange light above it. Once parked, visit our Venues page to obtain turn-by-turn walking directions to the Arts and Technology Building. If you'd like to avoid using the interactive campus map, simply walk west from PS1, go past the Davidson-Gundy Alumni Center, and enter the door on the east side of the ATC building (which faces Gundy). Walk down the hallway and ATC Lecture Hall will be on your left.

The Graduate Student Assembly (GSA) is the representative governing body of graduate students at UT Dallas. name: Comet Voice Suicide Prevention Training for Human Subjects Protections - Fall 2025/Spring 2026
description:
The Student Wellness Center and Office of Human Subjects Protections invite you to attend the Comet Voice Suicide Prevention Training for Human Subjects Protections. This training aims to equip attendees with essential knowledge and skills to effectively identify and respond to individuals at risk of suicide. You will learn the SAFER model for intervention, a structured approach designed to facilitate meaningful conversations and provide support to individuals in crisis. This model emphasizes understanding risk factors and warning signs of someone experiencing suicide ideation. By the end of this training, you will be better prepared to engage with and support individuals at risk, contributing to a community that prioritizes mental health and well-being.

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.
